dedupe_keys.name: england disruption of ambulance and fire service response to vulnerable people during floods

description: This case study measures how floods would slow ambulance and fire and rescue service responses to vulnerable people across England. The authors, researchers at Loughborough University, East China Normal University, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, Lausanne, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Princeton, Tsinghua and Hong Kong, modelled the spatial coverage of every Ambulance Service and Fire and Rescue Service station in England within mandatory response times, on road networks flooded by events of varying severity, and published the work in a journal article whose PDF is free to read online on the publisher's site. Coverage is England, with hotspots mapped locally. Caveats: travel times are modelled from road speeds and flood extents, not observed responses, and flood defences and service adaptations are simplified. The study found that even low-magnitude floods can reduce national compliance with mandatory response times, with more dramatic falls in some urban agglomerations, that centralisation of ambulance stations and decentralisation of fire stations underpin this sensitivity, and that hotspots such as care homes, sheltered accommodation, nurseries and schools can be identified for station siting and contingency plans. Simulation uses: a method and results for flood exposure of emergency service coverage and for station location and cover planning. Related records: the global thesis on flood impacts on emergency services (case_study-global-flood-impacts-emergency-service-accessibility-thesis) extends the method, and the German flood hospital access model (model-flood-traffic-hospital-access-germany) does the same for hospitals.
